analysis.one_liner: Bars colleges from forcing students into arbitration instead of court.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in two House committees for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop colleges that take federal student aid from requiring students to sign away their right to sue. Today, many students must agree as a condition of enrollment to settle any dispute—about fraud, broken promises, or poor teaching—in private arbitration, with no judge, no jury, and no class action. The bill would make those clauses unenforceable and make schools drop all limits on taking a college to court, individually or as a group. It was introduced by Rep. Maxine Waters with 13 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Education and the Workforce and Judiciary committees, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at colleges that participate in federal student aid programs—especially those with fraud or breach-of-contract claims against their school—would regain the right to file a case in court, have a jury decide it, and join class actions. The 2015 context included well-publicized lawsuits by students against for-profit colleges that mandatory-arbitration clauses could shut down.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students with claims against their college

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes federal arbitration-enforcement law (title 9, chapter 1 of the U.S. Code) inapplicable to enrollment agreements between a student and an institution of higher education, so a school could not enforce a forced-arbitration clause in the enrollment contract.

It adds a condition to the Higher Education Act: a college participating in federal student aid programs, including work-study, may not require or enforce any restriction—on choice of law, jury trial, or venue—on a student's ability to pursue a claim in court, individually or with others.
The restriction would take effect one year after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges—particularly for-profit schools that have relied on arbitration clauses to keep disputes out of court—would face lawsuits and class actions they currently can block, with the litigation costs and legal exposure that come with them. Arbitration providers would lose a stream of education-related cases.

drawbacks.text: Litigation is slower and more expensive than arbitration for a student with a small individual claim; without arbitration, some students might get less money after legal fees, and defenders of arbitration argue it can be faster and cheaper in ordinary commercial disputes.

Colleges warn that broader litigation exposure and class actions would raise costs that get passed to students or push schools out of federal aid programs, shrinking options for the very students the bill aims to protect.
The bill is written narrowly for higher education, so it would not touch the same forced-arbitration clauses in other consumer contracts, leaving the broader problem in place elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit—students with real claims (fraud, misrepresentation, broken degree promises) being able to reach a court and a jury—is meaningful, and the bill is tightly targeted at schools that take federal money, so schools could avoid it by simply not requiring the clauses. The honest cost is that individual lawsuits are expensive relative to the size of most student claims, and class actions capture only part of that gap; the burden lands mostly on schools with something to hide, but not only on them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a Judiciary subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the bill on April 28, 2015, with 13 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
The Speaker referred it to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and the Judiciary Committee, a split referral that gives each committee jurisdiction only over the parts in its area.

On June 26, 2015, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law; the record shows no further action, hearing, or vote through the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges—especially for-profit chains—kept the power to force disputes into private arbitration, and the arbitration industry kept the business. Students with claims against their schools got no relief.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action—no hearing, markup, or vote—for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee and its Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law

against.name: House Republican majority

sides.party_line_note: All 14 supporters (the sponsor plus 13 cosponsors) were Democrats and no Republican signed on, in a House where Republicans held the majority and controlled which bills got committee time.

industries.note: These schools have been the most frequent users of mandatory-arbitration clauses in enrollment contracts, using them to keep fraud and misrepresentation claims out of court and out of class actions. The bill's failure leaves that shield intact, which matters because students are often the only check on a school's recruiting promises.

Any college in federal aid programs that requires arbitration or limits on suits keeps the ability to block students' court claims. The bill would have made dropping such clauses a condition of federal aid.

The bill would have removed education enrollment contracts from the market for mandatory arbitration, so the bill's death preserves that business. Private arbitration also keeps disputes out of public court records, reducing visibility into college misconduct.
